months.6: The hurricane season begins with regular downpours and rising heat, making long treks harder work.

months.10: The snow line retreats, opening mid-elevation trails. The high passes on the multi-day tracks still hold snow, but lower day hikes become much more accessible.

months.5: Deepening snow and short daylight hours limit walking to the lowest coastal paths and valley floors. High routes are impassable without snow gear.
months.6: Deep snow covers the landscape, and walking is restricted to short, snowy strolls near Ushuaia or groomed snow paths. High trails are completely closed.
months.8: Snow remains deep across the region. Walking is confined to low-elevation snow paths, and the mountain trails are out of reach.

months.12: The first heavy rains of the wet months flood the salt flats, cutting off access to Isla Incahuasi and making most walking impossible.

peru.overview: Cusco and the Sacred Valley offer famous trekking, leading through the high Andes to ancient ruins. The multi-day routes are the main draw, led by the four-day Inca Trail to Machu Picchu, which needs a permit booked months ahead, and the demanding, high-altitude Salkantay trek past glacier-capped peaks. Day hikers can tackle the steep climb to Rainbow Mountain at over 16,000 feet, or explore shorter paths between Inca sites. The best conditions run from May to September, while heavy rains disrupt routes early in the year.
